covered.why: Establishes the boundary between agent, LLM call, and RAG pipeline — the starting point for every interview answer.
Provides the mental model for why ReAct/plan-and-execute work: the LLM plans, decides, and reflects, not just completes.
Interviewers expect fluency with tool schemas, parallel calls, and strict JSON — the primitive all patterns build on.
Agents emit structured actions; JSON mode/function calling enforces it. Needed to explain how frameworks guarantee parseable output.
Base pattern: must trace a single tool-use step (reason → act → observe) before explaining loops and multi-step patterns.
Canonical single-agent pattern; baseline for comparing plan-and-execute and multi-agent. Must trace the reasoning-acting loop.
Key architectural distinction: separates planning from execution. Interviewers probe trade-offs (flexibility vs control, latency, error recovery).
Standard follow-up: 'How does the agent recover from a bad tool call?' Covers Reflexion, ReWOO, self-critique loops.
Most common production pattern. Must trace delegation, compare with swarm, and explain framework implementations (LangGraph supervisor, CrewAI).
Contrast with supervisor: latency, coordination, failure modes. Interviewers ask 'when would you choose swarm over supervisor?'.
Advanced follow-up for scaling ('how to coordinate 50 agents?'). Keep at explain level — mental model, not deep trace.
AutoGen's signature pattern. Must explain *why* debate improves correctness (diverse reasoning paths, error catching) not just *that* it does.
Explicit deployment trade-off. Frameworks differ (LangGraph interrupt, AutoGen user proxy, OpenAI approvals). Must trace approval flow.
Target explicitly says 'trace execution through tool-use loops.' This IS the loop — state, messages, tool calls, returns.
LangGraph's differentiator; enables HITL, time-travel, recovery. 'How does your agent resume after a crash?' is a standard question.
Production reality: streaming tokens, progressive tool results, async tool calls. Explain UX and backend implications.
Practical follow-up: 'Tool fails — what happens?' Framework differences (LangGraph retry policy, CrewAI max_iter, AutoGen max_consecutive_auto_reply).
Memory follow-ups start here: context limits, history management, summarization strategies.
Past interactions/trajectories for personalization and few-shot. Distinct retrieval and storage from semantic.
Facts, docs, RAG — distinct from episodic in architecture and retrieval. Core to 'agent with RAG tool' vs 'RAG pipeline'.
Emerging concept (LangGraph skills, AutoGen skills). Mention for completeness; not yet standard interview territory.
Agents *use* RAG as a tool; interviewers blur the line. Must distinguish 'agent with RAG tool' from 'RAG pipeline' clearly.

covered.concept: Prompt Engineering for Agents (System Prompts, Few-Shot)
covered.why: Agents are prompt-heavy; system prompt defines personality, tool schemas, guardrails. 'Show me your system prompt' is a real ask.
Classic interview question: 'When would you use RAG vs an agent?' Must articulate retrieval vs reasoning+action cleanly.
Current standard for controllable, stateful, production-grade agents. Core of framework comparison — graph API, checkpointer, interrupts.
Role-based multi-agent, declarative, opinionated. Standard comparison point for 'when to use vs LangGraph'.
Conversation-centric, flexible multi-agent, strong on code execution and debate. Contrasts with LangGraph's explicit control.
Still in codebases/tutorials. 'What's wrong with the old agent executor?' tests understanding of LangGraph's improvements.
Standard multi-task benchmark; must know what it measures (planning, tool-use, reasoning) and its limitations.
Production teams build custom evals. Must explain LLM-as-judge, trajectory scoring, pass/fail criteria — not just benchmark names.
Cannot debug agents without traces. LangGraph/LangSmith integration is a major selling point interviewers expect you to know.
Enterprise interviews always ask safety. Guardrails vs framework-native controls (LangGraph interrupts, OpenAI moderation).

modules.title: Foundations: What Makes an Agent
modules.capability: Explain what distinguishes an agent from a plain LLM call or RAG pipeline, trace a single tool-use step (reason → act → observe), and describe the function calling API contract (schemas, parallel calls, strict JSON).
modules.why_here: These five concepts form the indivisible foundation: what an agent is, why the LLM can reason, the API primitive that enables tools, how structure is enforced, and the base tool-use step. Nothing later makes sense without this mental model, and they are tightly coupled — tool calling requires structured output, which requires function calling API, which requires the LLM-as-reasoner view.

modules.title: Core Single-Agent Patterns
modules.capability: Compare ReAct and plan-and-execute architectures across planning granularity, error recovery, latency, and control; trace a ReAct loop iteration; explain how reflection/self-correction loops (Reflexion, ReWOO) improve recovery from bad tool calls.
modules.why_here: ReAct and plan-and-execute are the two canonical single-agent architectures — interviewers compare them directly. Reflection is the standard recovery mechanism layered on top. They share the same execution substrate (tool-use loop) and are best learned as a contrast set before multi-agent adds coordination complexity.

modules.title: Agent Execution Mechanics
modules.capability: Trace execution through a complete tool-use loop including state updates, streaming tokens/progressive tool results, and error recovery paths; explain how checkpointing enables crash recovery, time-travel debugging, and human-in-the-loop approval gates.
modules.why_here: These four concepts are the runtime machinery: the loop itself, how state persists across steps, how output streams to users, and how failures are handled. They are framework-agnostic but directly determine framework capabilities (LangGraph's checkpointer, CrewAI's max_iter). Tracing execution — a target capability — requires all four together.

modules.title: Multi-Agent Architectures
modules.capability: Distinguish supervisor, swarm, hierarchical, and debate multi-agent topologies; justify a topology choice for a given scenario (latency, failure modes, coordination needs); trace how human approval gates integrate into each topology across frameworks.
modules.why_here: All five are coordination topologies for multiple agents. Supervisor, swarm, hierarchical, and debate form a complete contrast set — interviewers ask 'which topology for X?' Human-in-the-loop is included here because approval gates are a coordination pattern (human as a special agent) and frameworks implement HITL differently per topology (LangGraph interrupt vs AutoGen user proxy).

modules.title: Memory for Agents
covers: Prompt Engineering for Agents (System Prompts, Few-Shot)
modules.capability: Compare the three long-term memory types (episodic, semantic, procedural) and their retrieval strategies; distinguish an agent with a RAG tool from a RAG pipeline and justify when to use each; design a system prompt that defines agent personality, tool schemas, and guardrails.
modules.why_here: Memory is a cross-cutting concern but forms a coherent subsystem: working memory feeds the loop; three long-term types (episodic, semantic, procedural) have distinct storage/retrieval; RAG is a tool agents *use*; prompt engineering configures behavior; RAG-vs-agent is the classic distinction interviewers test. They belong together because memory decisions are made at architecture time, not per-pattern.

modules.title: Framework Comparison: LangGraph, CrewAI, AutoGen
modules.capability: Compare LangGraph, CrewAI, and AutoGen across control model (explicit graph vs declarative roles vs conversation), state management (checkpointer vs shared context vs chat history), multi-agent topology support, and HITL integration; explain why LangGraph replaced the legacy LangChain agent executor.
modules.why_here: These are the three frameworks interviewers expect you to compare deeply, plus the legacy LangChain agent as a contrast for 'why LangGraph'. They map directly to the patterns: LangGraph → graph-based control (ReAct, plan-and-execute, supervisor), CrewAI → role-based declarative (supervisor), AutoGen → conversation-centric (debate, swarm). Legacy LangChain shows what explicit state management solves.

modules.title: Other Frameworks & Evaluation
modules.capability: Position Semantic Kernel, OpenAI Assistants, and LlamaIndex relative to LangGraph/CrewAI/AutoGen by philosophy and use case; explain what AutoGPT got wrong historically; select an evaluation approach (benchmark suite vs custom LLM-as-judge) for a given agent use case and design a trajectory scoring rubric.
modules.why_here: Secondary frameworks (Semantic Kernel, OpenAI, LlamaIndex) are positioned relative to the big three — each represents a distinct philosophy (planner-centric, managed, RAG-first). Historical references (AutoGPT) explain evolution. Benchmarks (AgentBench + three named) and custom eval complete the evaluation story: what benchmarks measure vs what production teams actually build (LLM-as-judge, trajectory scoring).

modules.title: Deployment Trade-offs
covers: Cost & Latency Optimization (Model Selection, Caching, Token Budget)
modules.capability: Articulate deployment trade-offs for observability (trace-driven debugging vs logging), safety (external guardrails vs framework-native interrupts vs vendor moderation), and cost/latency (model cascade, caching, token budgets, routing); explain how each concern influences framework choice.
modules.why_here: These three are the production concerns interviewers probe as 'deployment trade-offs': observability (you can't debug without traces), safety (enterprise requirement), cost/latency (agents are expensive). They are framework-agnostic but framework-informed (LangSmith integration, LangGraph interrupts for guardrails, model routing for cost). Versioning and scaling are cut (see consequence).
